Calorimetry. A laboratory technique used to measure the amount of heat transferred to or from a substance during chemical reactions, physical changes, or phase transitions. It relies on a closed vessel called a calorimeter, which insulates the system from the environment, allowing researchers to calculate changes in internal energy or enthalpy by monitoring temperature changes.

Calorimeters come in several forms. Bomb calorimeters measure the heat of combustion of organic compounds under constant volume conditions, typically inside a pressurized steel vessel surrounded by water. For simpler aqueous reactions, coffee-cup calorimeters offer constant-pressure calorimetry—open-system containers often made of polystyrene that measure enthalpy changes.

More sophisticated instruments have specialized functions. Differential scanning calorimetry, or DSC, studies phase transitions by measuring the difference in heat flow between a sample and a reference as they are heated at a controlled rate. Isothermal titration calorimetry, used in biochemistry, determines the binding affinity, stoichiometry, and enthalpy changes of molecular interactions in solution.

The mathematics behind calorimetry is straightforward. Heat transfer is calculated using the specific heat capacity equation, where heat exchanged equals mass times specific heat capacity times temperature change. Water is the standard surrounding fluid in calorimeters due to its high and well-characterized specific heat capacity. In fact, measuring the caloric content of carbon-based foods and fuels is one of the most common applications of calorimetry, while bomb calorimeters themselves are filled with high-pressure oxygen gas to ensure the complete combustion of the sample.
